unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8. This unit is called "Media, Technology, and News" because you will explore how information travels in the modern world and why it matters to think critically about everything you read, watch, and share. Every day, millions of messages flow through newspapers, television channels, websites, and social media platforms. Some of these messages are carefully researched and truthful. Others are misleading, exaggerated, or completely false. As a young person growing up in the digital age, one of the most important skills you can develop is the ability to tell the difference between reliable information and misinformation.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary companion and learn the thirty unit words a few at a time, saying each example aloud. Work through the six grammar workshops, from present perfect and reported speech to conditionals, complex noun phrases and multi-word verbs. Read 'Media Literacy: Reading the News with Care' and 'Breaking News at Kilima Academy', then the two-part story 'The Duty of Truth', answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the writing workshop with the school magazine article and the fake news analysis, record the speaking tasks including the five-minute talk and the news broadcast, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: Media Literacy: Reading the News with Care
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every morning, long before the school gates open, the day's news is already moving. Radio presenters read bulletins, television studios broadcast interviews, newspapers roll off the presses, and millions of messages travel between phones in seconds. Some of this information has been carefully researched and checked. Some of it is exaggerated, one-sided or simply invented. Media literacy is the skill of understanding how news is made, judging how reliable it is, and sharing it responsibly. In the digital age, that skill has become a necessity, not a luxury.
To judge the news, it helps to understand how serious journalism works. A professional reporter does not publish the first thing she hears. She interviews people who saw the event, takes copious notes, and keeps a record of every conversation. An editor then questions her draft, checks the facts and removes anything the evidence cannot support. Important stories are often checked for several consecutive days before they are published. Reliable news organisations also print their reporters' names, welcome opposition from readers who disagree, and correct their mistakes publicly. Most modern newsrooms are hybrid operations, producing a printed edition and a website at the same time, but careful checking remains a component of both.
It also helps to know the difference between news and opinion. A news report should describe what happened and support every claim with evidence. An opinion column exists to express a viewpoint and to persuade. Good publications label the two clearly, because a reader who cannot tell them apart will treat every strong opinion as a fact.
Unreliable sources behave differently. They hide behind anonymous accounts, publish claims without evidence, and use dramatic capital letters and emotional language to influence readers instead of informing them. A story that appears abruptly, from an account with no history and no author's name, deserves suspicion. So does a headline that tries to convince you before you have read a single fact. Misinformation is a chronic problem on social media because false stories are often more exciting than true ones, and excitement spreads faster than accuracy.
Fortunately, you do not need special equipment to defend yourself. You need three questions. First, who is making this claim, and are they named? Second, what evidence supports it: a document, a named witness, an official statement? Third, does the report correspond with what trusted sources are saying? If a dramatic story appears nowhere except one unnamed account, that silence is itself a warning sign.
There is an old East African proverb that says, 'A rumour runs fast, but the truth builds the house.' A rumour costs nothing to start and spreads in minutes; the truth takes patient, industrious work to establish. When you pause before sharing, check the source and wait for evidence, you are doing the quiet work of building. Every reader who refuses to pass on an unverified claim makes the whole community harder to fool, and that may be the most valuable development of all.

readings.title: Breaking News at Kilima Academy
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
It was a Tuesday morning when Rohan first saw the message on his phone. Someone had posted a video on social media claiming that Kilima Academy would be shut down at the end of the month. The video showed a blurry photograph of a letter supposedly from the Ministry of Education, and a voice said, "This school has failed its inspection. All students must find new schools immediately."
Within minutes, the message had been shared hundreds of times. Parents began calling the school in a panic. Some students arrived at the gates looking worried, asking their friends if the news was true. Rohan's younger sister Tia ran to him during the morning break, her eyes wide with fear.
"Is it true?" she asked. "Are they closing our school?"
Rohan looked at the video again carefully. Something about it did not feel right. The letter in the photograph was blurry, and he could not see an official stamp or signature. The voice in the video belonged to someone he did not recognise, and there was no name or source given. He remembered what his English teacher, Mr. Nadir, had taught them about evaluating sources: always check who is making the claim, look for evidence, and verify information before sharing it.
"I do not think this is real," Rohan told Tia. "But let us find out for certain."
During the lunch break, Rohan gathered a small group of students from the school's journalism club. They decided to investigate the rumour systematically. First, they visited the school office and asked the administrator directly. The administrator confirmed that no such letter existed and that the school had passed its most recent inspection with excellent marks. She even showed them the real inspection report.
Next, Imani, the club's best researcher, searched the Ministry of Education's official website. There was no announcement about closing any school in their district. She also checked the accounts that had shared the original video and noticed they were all very new accounts with no other posts, which is a common sign of a deliberate misinformation campaign.
The journalism club wrote a short, clear article for the school noticeboard and the school's messaging group. They included three pieces of evidence: a quote from the administrator, a link to the official inspection results, and an explanation of why the video was not trustworthy. They also added a helpful list of tips for spotting fake news, such as checking the source, looking for official evidence, and waiting before sharing unverified information.
By the end of the day, the panic had calmed. Parents who had been worried sent messages of thanks. The headteacher praised the journalism club in the next assembly and said, "These students have shown us that the best response to false information is not fear or anger. It is careful investigation, clear communication, and the truth."
Rohan felt proud. He had learned something important that day: in the age of social media, everyone has a responsibility to check information before they believe it or share it. The truth does not spread by itself. It needs people who care enough to find it and share it responsibly.

readings.title: The Duty of Truth, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The first day back after the mid-term break started with a murmur in the halls of Bahari Secondary School. Everyone was talking about the new rule that had been posted abruptly on the school notice board: "All Form 3 students must now report for Saturday cleaning duty. Attendance is mandatory."
Zara stood reading the notice, arms folded. She was the liaison between the student council and the school board — a role that required calm thinking and strong communication.
"They've added a new duty without asking anyone," she muttered. "No explanation. No vote."
"I heard it was the deputy head teacher's idea," said Kian, her classmate. "Apparently he wants to punish us for being 'lazy' during the last clean-up day."
"But that's not true," Zara said. "Our class actually contributed the most."
During lunch, the student council held an emergency meeting. As they gathered under the neem tree, Zara pulled out her notebook.
"We need to respond," she said. "Either we accept this quietly, or we challenge it the right way."
Their secretary, Dina, raised her hand. "Let's write a formal letter requesting an amendment to the rule."
"But who will sign it?" asked Milo.
"Everyone," said Zara. "If we want to be taken seriously."
They agreed to organise a petition. Meanwhile, Zara offered to consult the deputy head teacher for more explanation.
She visited his office that afternoon.
"We've just received complaints from parents," he said. "So we added the duty to teach accountability."
"Sir, the students weren't even informed. The rule appeared overnight."
"The board agreed. It is a necessary policy."
"But it feels more like punishment than learning."
He leaned back. "It's not up for debate."
Back outside, Zara sighed. She was beginning to realise that being a delegate wasn't just about passing messages — it was about standing firm.
That evening, she and Dina drafted a letter:
To the School Board: We request an amendment to the newly posted Saturday rule. We feel the decision was made without student input. We suggest an alternate plan where duty is shared across all forms, or rotated biweekly.
They included a list of students who had contributed to the last clean-up. It was clear: Form 3 had not been negligent.
By Friday, over 200 students had signed the petition. It was submitted to the principal's office.
That weekend, instead of cleaning, the students held a quiet assembly in the school field, holding signs that read "Shared Duty is Fair Duty."
The following Monday, a notice appeared: The Saturday duty rule has been paused. A review is underway.
Zara smiled. "That's progress."
But the story didn't end there.
The school board called for a student representative to attend their monthly meeting. Zara was chosen.
She entered the conference room where teachers, community leaders, and government officials sat. The atmosphere was formal. She was nervous, but ready.
A senior board member asked, "Miss Zara, why are students opposed to the cleaning rule?"
She stood and replied, "We are not opposed to cleaning. We are opposed to unfair allocation of tasks. Either all students share the duty, or it becomes a punishment. That is unjust."
Another member raised a paper. "But an anonymous teacher alleges that students in Form 3 have skipped duty before."
"That's a claim," Zara said. "But we provided logs showing our participation."

readings.title: The Duty of Truth, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The principal cleared his throat. "Actually, the student records indicate that Form 3 cleaned more consecutively than other forms."
A silence followed.
"Well," one board member said, "this is a good example of democratic dialogue."
A proposal was made to delegate cleaning duties in a rotating system. Zara helped draft the new schedule.
Later that day, she met with her classmates.
"We did it. The rule has been changed."
"You were amazing," said Dina. "Your voice really influenced them."
Zara shrugged. "I think the facts did. I just helped present them."
The news spread fast. Students felt more eligible to speak up now. Others who had felt ignored started joining meetings. The school felt more united.
The English teacher, Mr. Kofi, was especially proud.
He said, "Zara has shown us the power of communication. This is not just about a rule — it's about how rules are made."
As part of an assignment, Zara wrote a report titled Civic Responsibility in School Spaces. In it, she explained how one small act can lead to big development.
She concluded: "It is important to question rules that are imposed without consulting those they affect. Students are not just followers. They are also citizens."
Meanwhile, another issue came up. A student had been accused of vandalising a locker. But no one saw it happen.
"He's liable," said one prefect. "He was nearby."
"But that's not proof," Zara said. "You can't punish someone on what's alleged."
They held a hearing. After testimonies were reviewed, the boy was exonerated. It turned out a loose screw had caused the damage.
The experience left a mark.
"From now on," said Zara, "let's rely on facts, not fear."
By the end of term, the student council had created a newsletter. They corresponded regularly with the board. More students became industrious, organising events, tutoring, and contributing to school improvement.
The school even tried a hybrid student-teacher planning group to create future policies.
And as Zara looked over the minutes of their last meeting, she smiled.
Progress isn't just about big speeches. It's about organising voices, balancing rights and rules, and believing that structure can serve justice.
Even when it starts with a mop and a notice board.

grammar.title: Present Perfect + Just, and Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: The present perfect with just announces that something happened moments ago, which is why news reports say, "The government has just announced a new policy." Reported speech then lets a journalist pass on what someone said without quoting every word. Together, these two patterns are the engine room of news English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form the present perfect with have or has plus a past participle, and place just before the participle: "They have just completed the project." "She has just been exonerated." Use have with I, you, we and they; use has with he, she and it. Make the negative by adding not ("He has not just arrived") and make a question by swapping the subject and have or has ("Has she just called?").
To turn direct speech into reported speech, remove the quotation marks, add that after the reporting verb, and step the tense back one: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, will becomes would and can becomes could. Change pronouns and time words to fit the reporter, so Rohan said, "I do not think this is real" becomes Rohan said that he did not think it was real, and tomorrow becomes the next day. Choose the reporting verb carefully: said is neutral, told needs a person, explained gives reasons, claimed signals doubt, admitted concedes, denied rejects and warned alerts.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the wrong form of have ("He have just finished"), pairing just with the wrong participle ("They have just go"), or forgetting to shift the tense in reported speech ("She said that she does not think it is real").
grammar.memoryTip: Just is a little alarm bell — this happened moments ago, pay attention — and it always sits right before the past participle; when you report speech, step back one tense, like retelling yesterday's story.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with have or has, just and the verb in brackets: 1) I ______ (see) the new noticeboard. 2) They ______ (finish) their lunch. 3) She ______ (receive) a letter. 4) The reporter ______ (publish) the article.
Part B — rewrite each sentence in reported speech: 5) Rohan said, "I do not believe this video is real." 6) The administrator told them, "The school has passed its inspection." 7) Imani said, "I will search the official website tomorrow." 8) The headteacher announced, "These students have shown great responsibility." 9) Tia asked, "Are they closing our school?"
Part C — write one sentence in reported speech recording something your teacher said this week.

=== Self-Check Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) have just seen 2) have just finished 3) has just received 4) has just published.
Part B: 5) Rohan said that he did not believe the video was real. 6) The administrator told them that the school had passed its inspection. 7) Imani said that she would search the official website the next day. 8) The headteacher announced that those students had shown great responsibility. 9) Tia asked if/whether they were closing their school.
Part C is a personal response, so there is no single correct sentence. Self-check by confirming: quotation marks are removed, the tense steps back one (present becomes past, present perfect becomes past perfect, will becomes would), pronouns and time words are adjusted to fit who is reporting, and a suitable reporting verb is used (said, told, explained, admitted, etc.). Model example: if your teacher said, "We will have a spelling test on Friday," you could write: My teacher said that we would have a spelling test on Friday.

grammar.title: Connectives and Conditionals
grammar.explanation: Connectives such as because, so that, therefore and although show how one idea relates to another, while conditional sentences with if let writers weigh what is likely, imaginary or avoidable. News writing leans on both to build logical, balanced arguments.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use because to give a reason ("I wore my raincoat because it was raining"), so that for purpose ("I studied hard so that I could pass the test"), therefore for a conclusion ("It was very cold; therefore, we stayed inside") and although for contrast ("Although it was raining, we went for a walk"). When the connective opens the sentence, follow its clause with a comma.
The first conditional describes real, likely possibilities: if plus present simple, then will plus the base verb — "If you check the source, you will know whether the news is real." The second conditional describes imaginary or unlikely situations: if plus past simple, then would plus the base verb — "If everyone verified information before sharing it, there would be much less misinformation." In formal writing, prefer were for every subject: "If I were a journalist, I would always check my facts." The if-clause may come first or second; use a comma only when it comes first.
grammar.commonMistake: Confusing because (reason) with so that (purpose), and putting will in both halves of a conditional — "If I will check the source, I will know the truth" should keep the present simple in the if-clause.
grammar.memoryTip: Connectives are bridges between ideas, and the comma is the small step just after you cross; for conditionals, allow one will per sentence, never two.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill each blank with because, so that, therefore or although: 1) I wanted to go outside, ______ it was raining. 2) She studied hard, ______ she could get good grades. 3) It was a sunny day; ______, we decided to have a picnic. 4) The cat meowed loudly ______ it was hungry.
Part B — decide first or second conditional and complete each sentence: 5) If you ______ (check) the source, you ______ (know) whether the news is real. 6) If social media ______ (not exist), fake news ______ (not spread) so quickly. 7) If the journalist ______ (verify) the story, she ______ (publish) it tomorrow. 8) If I ______ (be) the editor, I ______ (never publish) an article without checking the facts. 9) If people ______ (share) the correction, the truth ______ (reach) everyone by tonight.
Part C — write one original second conditional sentence imagining a world without social media.

=== Self-Check Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) although 2) so that 3) therefore 4) because.
Part B (first conditional = present simple + will; second conditional = past simple + would): 5) check / will know (first conditional) 6) did not exist / would not spread (second conditional) 7) verifies / will publish (first conditional) 8) were / would never publish (second conditional) 9) share / will reach (first conditional).
Part C is open-ended — your own idea about a world without social media. Self-check using the second conditional pattern: if + past simple, + would + base verb, describing something imaginary or unlikely, with only one would in the sentence. Model example: If social media did not exist, people would rely more on newspapers and television for their news.

grammar.title: Both, Either, and Neither
grammar.explanation: Both, either and neither manage pairs — two newspapers, two versions of a story, two sides of a debate — so they appear constantly in comparison and discussion.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Both refers to two things together and takes a plural noun and verb: "Both newspapers reported the story." "Both reports are accurate." Either selects one of two options: "You can read either the online version or the print version." Neither rejects both options and always pairs with nor, never with or: "Neither the headline nor the article was accurate." "Neither the reporter nor the editor checked the facts." When either or neither refers to one of two, the verb stays singular: "Either option is fine."
grammar.commonMistake: Pairing both with or — "You can have both ice cream or cake" should use either — and writing neither with or instead of nor, as in "Neither the cats or the dogs are here."
grammar.memoryTip: Both says two together, either says one of two, neither says none of two — and neither always brings its partner nor.

=== Self-Check Answer Key ===
1) either (one of two pens) 2) Both (mum and dad together, plural verb) 3) Neither (pairs with nor, rejects both) 4) Both (both versions together, plural verb).

grammar.title: The Past Continuous Tense
grammar.explanation: The past continuous describes what was already happening at a moment in the past. News writers use it to set the scene behind an event: "The students were discussing the article when the bell rang."
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Form it with was or were plus the -ing form of the verb. Use was with singular subjects: "She was reading the newspaper." Use were with plural subjects: "They were consulting their lawyer when they received the bad news." Two background actions can run side by side: "While I was studying, my brother was playing video games." A sudden event that interrupts the background takes the past simple: "The reporter was writing the article when the new information arrived."
grammar.commonMistake: Matching the wrong helper to the subject ("They was playing football") or dropping the -ing from the main verb ("She was read a book").
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a camera already rolling: was or were plus -ing is the film running in the background when something else suddenly happens.

=== Self-Check Answer Key ===
1) was watching / was cooking (two background actions running side by side) 2) were playing / started (background action interrupted by a sudden past simple event) 3) was writing / was drawing (two background actions side by side).

grammar.title: Complex Noun Phrases
grammar.explanation: A complex noun phrase packs adjectives, prepositional phrases and clauses around one noun, letting a reporter fit a paragraph of information into a single line — a skill headline writers depend on.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Build outward from the noun: start with "article", add an adjective ("a detailed article"), add a prepositional phrase ("a detailed article about media literacy"), then a relative clause ("a detailed article about media literacy that was published yesterday"). News writing is full of them: "a legally binding amendment to the school policy", "an industrious group of delegates who worked hard to reach an agreement", "the widely shared video claiming that the school would close", "a well-researched investigation carried out by the student journalism club". Keep adjectives in natural order — "the big blue balloon", never "the blue big balloon" — and resist piling up more describing words than the sentence needs.
grammar.commonMistake: Reversing adjective order ("the blue big balloon") or stacking empty intensifiers ("the really very big giant dog") instead of choosing one precise adjective.
grammar.memoryTip: Grow the phrase like a snowball: noun first, then roll on an adjective, a prepositional phrase and a relative clause, one layer at a time.

grammar.title: Adjective + Infinitive, Gerunds, and Multi-Word Verbs
grammar.explanation: Three verb patterns dominate media English: adjective plus infinitive states judgements about actions ("It is important to verify information"), the -ing form lets a verb act as a noun ("Reading the news daily improves your vocabulary"), and multi-word verbs such as look into and find out carry much of everyday reporting.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Adjective + infinitive follows It plus is or was plus adjective plus to plus verb: "It is necessary to consult a lawyer." "He was eligible to vote." "It was difficult to understand the complex article." Common adjectives in this pattern include necessary, happy, excited, eligible, difficult, important and easy.
The gerund adds -ing to the base verb — drop a final -e (write becomes writing) and double a short final consonant (run becomes running). It works as a subject ("Reading the news every day improves your vocabulary"), as an object ("She avoided expressing bias in her article"), after a preposition ("They talked about allocating resources fairly") and after verbs such as enjoy, avoid, suggest and consider ("He enjoys researching current events").
Multi-word verbs pair a verb with a particle whose combined meaning is new: find out (discover), look into (investigate), turn out (prove to be), come across (find by chance), point out (draw attention to), make up (invent), pass on (share), bring up (raise a topic), set up (establish) and carry out (perform). Some are separable — "She found the truth out" or "She found out the truth" — but inseparable ones keep the particle beside the verb: "The students looked into the rumour", never "looked the rumour into".
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping to after the adjective ("He was eligible vote"), using the infinitive where the -ing form belongs ("interested to learn" instead of "interested in learning"), and splitting an inseparable multi-word verb ("The students looked the rumour into").
grammar.memoryTip: Judgements take to ("important to check"); after prepositions and verbs like enjoy and avoid, reach for -ing; and treat an inseparable phrasal verb as one glued word.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete with the adjective and infinitive: 1) It is ______ (necessary / consult) a doctor when you feel unwell. 2) She is ______ (excited / visit) her grandparents. 3) It is ______ (important / check) news sources before sharing.
Part B — use the correct -ing form: 4) I love ______ (read) the news every morning. 5) They are excited about ______ (travel) this summer. 6) She avoided ______ (share) the unverified article. 7) We talked about ______ (organise) a school newspaper.
Part C — fill each gap with the correct multi-word verb from find out, look into, turn out, point out, make up, pass on, set up and carry out: 8) The journalism club decided to ______ the rumour before writing their article. 9) Someone had completely ______ the story about the school closing. 10) The students ______ a noticeboard article to share the truth. 11) The teacher ______ that the video had no official stamp or signature. 12) The fake story ______ to be a deliberate attempt to cause panic. 13) Please do not ______ unverified information to your friends and family. 14) The reporter ______ a thorough investigation before publishing the story. 15) We need to ______ the facts before we can write an accurate report.

=== Self-Check Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) necessary to consult 2) excited to visit 3) important to check.
Part B: 4) reading 5) travelling (or travelling) 6) sharing 7) organising.
Part C: 8) look into 9) made up 10) set up 11) pointed out 12) turned out 13) pass on 14) carried out 15) find out.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Debate: Digital Media Ethics
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: A debate is a structured discussion in which two sides argue for and against a statement. Choose one topic: 'Social media does more harm than good for young people', 'Schools should teach media literacy as a compulsory subject', 'People who deliberately spread fake news should face legal consequences', or 'Everyone has the right to post whatever they want online, even if it is not true.' Divide into two teams, give each speaker one to two minutes, use at least one opinion phrase such as 'I believe' or 'In my opinion', and begin any disagreement with a polite phrase such as 'I see your point, but I think that...'. writing.title: Writing 1: School Magazine Article
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine your school has just launched its first student magazine and you are one of its reporters. Write an article of 200-300 words about a recent event at your school or in your community — a new club, a charity collection, a guest speaker, a debate about a school rule, or a topic of your own. Follow the conventions of good journalism: a short, accurate, attention-grabbing headline; a lead paragraph answering the five Ws (who, what, when, where, why); at least one direct quote with correct punctuation; at least one sentence of reported speech; factual, balanced language; and a concluding sentence that sums up or looks ahead.
writing.modelText:
Kilima Academy Launches Debate Club
Students at Kilima Academy have just started the school's first debate club. Twenty-four pupils met in the library on Friday 3 May to organise weekly sessions, because many wanted a place to express opinions and consult others before big decisions.
"Debating teaches you to check a claim before you repeat it," said Rohan, the club's liaison with staff.
Mrs Adan, who supervises the club, said that attendance was not mandatory but that copious sign-ups had already arrived.
The club's first public debate is planned for June.
writing.sentenceStarter: Students at our school have just...
writing.expectedLength: Three to four organised paragraphs (200-300 words)

items: Headline: New Recycling Club Launches at Green Valley School

Lead paragraph (five Ws): Students at Green Valley Secondary School launched a new recycling club on Tuesday 14 April, meeting in Classroom 6 after school finished, because several pupils wanted a practical way to reduce the litter building up around the football pitch.
Direct quote: "We were tired of watching plastic bottles blow across the pitch every break time," said Amina, the club's founding member. "Now we actually have somewhere to put them."

Reported speech, balanced language: Mr Farah, the club's supervising teacher, said that although the club was entirely voluntary, more than thirty students had already signed up in the first week. Not every pupil is convinced the club will last, and some students pointed out that similar projects have fizzled out before once the initial excitement faded.
Concluding sentence: The club's first collection day is planned for the end of the month, and organisers hope the early enthusiasm turns into a habit that outlasts the novelty.
otherAnswers: A learner reporting on a guest speaker might lead with "A local doctor visited Year 8 on Monday to talk about nutrition," quote one memorable line from the talk, and close by naming the follow-up workshop planned for next term.
A learner reporting on a debate about school rules might lead with the exact motion debated, quote a speaker from each side in reported speech, and close by naming the date of the staff decision.

writing.title: Writing 2: Fake News Analysis
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Analyse this fake claim: 'BREAKING: The government has announced that all schools will switch to online-only learning permanently starting next month. A source close to the Ministry confirmed the plan.' Write clear paragraphs answering these questions: Who is the source, and why does it matter that no one is named? What evidence is offered — any document, statement or data? How does the sensational language work as a warning sign? Could you confirm the story on any official or trusted source, and what does that absence suggest? Who could be harmed if it were shared unchecked? Finish with a correction of three to four sentences that you could post to help others understand why the claim is false.
writing.modelText:
The first warning sign in this claim is the source. "A source close to the Ministry" has no name or title, so nobody is liable if it is false and nobody can check it.
No evidence is offered: no document, statement or data. Words like BREAKING and permanently are chosen to alarm, and alarmed people share abruptly instead of checking.
The Ministry's website and the national broadcaster carry nothing that corresponds to it, which indicates the story was invented. Panicking parents and pupils would be the ones harmed.
Correction: This claim is false. The Ministry has announced no plan to move schools online permanently, and no official source confirms it. Please check the Ministry's website before sharing.
writing.sentenceStarter: The first warning sign in this claim is...
writing.expectedLength: Three analytical paragraphs plus a short correction paragraph

items: Source: The first warning sign in this claim is the source. "A source close to the Ministry" has no name or title, so nobody is liable if the claim turns out to be false, and nobody outside the story can actually check where it came from.

Evidence and language: No evidence is offered anywhere in the claim: no document, no official statement and no data are named. Words like BREAKING and permanently are chosen to alarm the reader, and alarmed people tend to share a story abruptly instead of pausing to check it first.

Confirmation and harm: Neither the Ministry's website nor the national broadcaster carries anything that corresponds to this announcement, which strongly indicates the story was invented rather than reported. Parents who suddenly stop sending their children to school, and pupils who panic about missed exams, would be the ones harmed if this claim spread unchecked.

Correction: This claim is false. The Ministry has announced no plan to move schools to online-only learning, and no official, named source confirms it. Please check the Ministry's website directly before sharing anything like this with your family.

writing.title: Writing 4: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Reread the story line 'Progress is not just about big speeches. It is about organising voices.' First write a short paragraph explaining what this line means to you and how it connects to your own life. Then choose one earlier piece of writing from this unit, revise three sentences to make them clearer, add two useful details, and explain one improvement you made and why it helps the reader.
writing.modelText:
To me, organising voices means turning many quiet complaints into one clear, evidence-based request. When my class wanted a later homework deadline, one loud speech changed nothing, but a short list of reasons we all signed convinced our teacher.
In my news report I revised this sentence: "The rule was bad and students were angry." It now reads: "The rule was posted abruptly, without consultation, and Form 3 students felt they were being blamed unfairly." I also added the date of the meeting and the fact that the records had exonerated Form 3.
The new sentence is clearer because it gives the reader a specific reason instead of a vague opinion.
writing.expectedLength: Two organised paragraphs plus a short reflection paragraph

items: Meaning and connection to my life: To me, organising voices means turning many small, scattered complaints into one clear, evidence-based request that is hard to ignore. When my class wanted permission to eat lunch outside on hot days, one loud complaint from a single student changed nothing, but a short written proposal signed by the whole class, listing our actual reasons, finally convinced our head of year.

Revisions from earlier work: In my news report I revised this sentence: "The rule was bad and students were angry." It now reads: "The rule was posted abruptly, without any consultation, and Form 3 students felt they were being blamed unfairly for a mess they had not caused." I also added the exact date of the board meeting and the fact that school records had cleared Form 3 of any special responsibility.
Reflection on the improvement: The new sentence is clearer because it replaces a vague opinion with specific, checkable reasons, which is exactly the kind of evidence a careful reader is looking for.

writing.title: Writing 5: Diary of the Liaison
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a diary entry of 100-150 words from Zara's point of view on the evening after the board meeting. writing.modelText:
Tonight I keep thinking about the moment I walked into the conference room. My hands were shaking, and the board members were sitting behind a long polished table. I felt small, but I had my facts and the petition, and I made myself express each point slowly.
When the principal checked the records, he said that Form 3 had cleaned more consecutively than any other form. One board member said it was a good example of democratic dialogue. I have learned that standing firm means being prepared, not loud, and refusing to give up when the facts are on your side.

writing.title: Writing 6: Information Text — How to Spot Fake News
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a heading and five accurate, ordered tips that teach a reader how to spot fake news. Draw on both reading passages, use at least four unit words such as claim, allege, indicate and correspond, and check your spelling and punctuation before you finish.
writing.modelText:
How to Spot Fake News
1. Before you share a story, first ask who is making the claim. A named reporter or official can be held liable; "a source close to" someone cannot.
2. Look for evidence. A real report shows a document, a statement or data, not just what somebody alleges.
3. Notice the language: BREAKING and capital letters indicate that the writer wants a reaction, not understanding.
4. Check whether the story corresponds to what trusted sources say, such as the Ministry's website or the school office.
5. If you cannot confirm it, do not pass it on. One blurry video caused a whole morning of panic at Kilima Academy.
writing.sentenceStarter: Before you share a story, first...
writing.expectedLength: An organised information paragraph with a heading

items: Heading: How to Spot Fake News
Tip one: Before you share a story, first ask who is making the claim. A named reporter or official can be held liable for what they say; "a source close to" someone cannot.
Tip two: Look for evidence. A real report points to a document, a statement or data, not just something somebody alleges without proof.
Tip three: Notice the language. Words in capital letters and phrases like BREAKING indicate that the writer wants a fast reaction, not careful understanding.
Tip four: Check whether the story corresponds to what trusted sources say, such as an official website or a national broadcaster, before you believe it.
Tip five: If you cannot confirm a claim anywhere trustworthy, do not pass it on. A single unchecked message caused a whole afternoon of panic at one school after a similar rumour spread.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Media, Technology, and News" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'express'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Explain what media literacy means and why it is important for young people today.
Identify the key features of a reliable news source and an unreliable one.
Read a text about media and answer comprehension and analysis questions in full sentences.
Use reported speech correctly to report what someone said or wrote.
Recognise and use common multi-word verbs (phrasal verbs) related to media and communication.
Form and use first and second conditional sentences to discuss possibilities and consequences.
Write a school magazine article that follows journalistic conventions such as headlines, leads, and quotes.
Analyse a piece of fake news and explain why it is unreliable, using specific evidence.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Media Literacy: Reading the News with Care" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Duty of Truth, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Present Perfect + Just, and Reported Speech" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
